Modulation. The act of changing from one key to another within a piece of music, creating harmonic variety and narrative momentum. It is a central technique in tonal music, allowing composers to explore related and distant harmonic regions before returning to the home key, deepening emotional and structural interest.

Pivot-chord modulation, also called common-chord modulation, uses a single chord that belongs to both the old and new key, easing the transition. This is the most common and smooth method. Direct or abrupt modulation simply shifts to a new key without preparatory chords, used for dramatic effect or surprise. A tonicization is a temporary emphasis on a non-tonic chord, making it sound like a temporary key, without fully committing to a new key. This technique is useful for local color and harmonic variety.

The development section of a sonata form modulates extensively through a series of keys, generating restlessness that propels the music toward recapitulation. Modulation from a minor key to its relative major, or vice versa, requires no accidental adjustments, as they share a key signature. Understanding how keys relate through their signatures is essential for successful modulation. Modulation operates within the major and minor tonal system and is the essential technique for harmonic motion in the development section. Adjacent keys on the circle of fifths are the easiest to modulate into.
